source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, banana cultivation techniques manual, 2019, section V.2.1 (corm/root weevil)
text:
The banana corm weevil (Cosmopolites sordidus) is a nocturnal beetle, shiny black and roughly 1cm long, that hides in plant debris and leaf litter during the day. Adults lay shiny white, oval eggs in cracks or wounds near the base of the pseudostem; eggs hatch in about 6-7 days into legless, white, brown-headed grubs roughly 1.5cm long that bore into and tunnel through the corm to feed. Plantations with accumulated dead leaf and stem debris around the base provide ideal hiding and breeding conditions for adult weevils.

Damage and impact: larval tunneling through the corm damages the tissue that transports water and nutrients, weakening the plant's anchorage so that it can topple in wind, especially once carrying a heavy fruit bunch; the wounds created by tunneling can also let in secondary rot organisms. Because the damage occurs underground, it is often not noticed until the plant is already showing wilting, stunting, or has fallen over.

Prevention and control: keep the plantation clear of dead stem and leaf debris where weevils hide; select only healthy, pest-free planting material; remove field debris promptly; after harvest, cut down the spent pseudostem right away and split it open to expose the interior to sunlight, which helps kill any larvae inside; set out trap pieces of cut banana stem to lure adult weevils, then collect and destroy them; and dust cut corm surfaces with ash to discourage weevils from laying eggs there.
